criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Memo identifies ELUR conflict with ground-floor residential use
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly identifies the conflict. Top-Risk Register item 9 states the ELUR prohibits ground-floor residential use while the program includes a ground-floor residential lobby and amenities. Section III.F.2 quotes the ELUR recorded March 22, 2018 at Volume 412, Page 88, prohibiting 'residential use on the ground floor of any structure erected on the land,' and directly contrasts it with Term Sheet Section 4(a)'s reference to 'ground-floor residential lobby and amenity spaces (fitness center, package room, resident lounge, and leasing office),' noting the instrument is internally inconsistent. The conflict is also carried into Issue Register item 28 and Conflict Register C19, with drafting responses (DEEP interpretation/modification as a condition precedent, non-habitable ground-floor uses, affordable units on upper floors). The contamination context (Phase II, ELUR, remediation) is discussed as well.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Lease defines permitted residential use to exclude ground-floor habitable space
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease explicitly addresses the ELUR ground-floor restriction. Section 3.9 prohibits 'residential use' on the ground floor and permits only non-habitable ground-floor uses such as retail, lobbies, mechanical rooms, parking, and non-habitable amenity space unless DEEP confirms otherwise. Section 3.6(c) further states that all dwelling units, including Affordable Housing Units, must be located above the ground floor. Exhibit E also restricts residential units to floors 2 through 28. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Affordable housing units specified for upper floors only
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.6(c) expressly addresses floor placement: it acknowledges the ELUR restricts ground-floor residential use and states that 'all Affordable Housing Units (and all other dwelling units) shall be located on floors above the ground floor of the Residential Tower,' with a cross-reference to Section 3.9. Exhibit E also states the Affordable Housing Units are located above the ground floor (Section 3.6). This fully satisfies the criterion of specifying upper-floor placement to comply with the ELUR restriction.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Memo identifies mechanics' lien as title defect requiring resolution
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly identifies the $187,500 mechanics' lien filed by Calloway Marine Demolition Inc. as a title defect requiring resolution. It appears in the Top-Risk Register (#12, described as improperly treated as a Permitted Exception), in Section V Conflict C5 (Term Sheet §13 vs. Title Commitment Ex. 6/Req. 7, noting the Title Company will not issue a policy until discharged), in Issue Register Item 18 (recommending discharge or bond as a condition precedent, exclusion from Permitted Exceptions, indemnity, and offset remedy), in Section 8.1 as workstream item 2, and in Appendix A with the exact recording citation 'Vol. 418, Pg. 302, filed April 3, 2025.' Appendix B likewise lists it as a departure from the Term Sheet. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Lease requires Authority to discharge mechanics' lien as condition precedent or provides indemnity
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly places the burden of clearing the Calloway Marine Demolition mechanics' lien on the Authority/Landlord. Section 2.7(c) makes delivery of evidence that the lien has been discharged of record or bonded off under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 49-37 a condition precedent to the Commencement Date. Section 15.4 separately obligates Landlord to discharge or bond off the $187,500 lien on or before the Commencement Date and expressly provides that 'Landlord shall indemnify Tenant against all loss arising from such lien,' with Tenant backup remedies (postponement, self-help discharge with offset). Exhibit B expressly excludes the lien from the Permitted Exceptions, and Section 15.2 again requires Landlord to remove it at its sole cost as a condition precedent. This satisfies the criterion (discharge as condition precedent and indemnity).

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Memo identifies rent calculation rounding discrepancy
ISSUE_003: Lease specifies which rent figure controls (lump sum vs. per-SF rate)
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease's Base Rent provision (Section 4.1) states the annual Base Rent is the lump sum of $2,850,000 and expressly provides that Base Rent 'is a flat dollar amount and shall not be recalculated, increased, or reduced by reference to the actual area of the Premises.' The per-SF rate of $20.45 never appears in the document; only the $2,850,000 lump sum figure is used, and the drafting notes reiterate that the fixed dollar amount controls regardless of surveyed or assessed area. The criterion is therefore satisfied by using only one of the two figures and by designating the lump sum as controlling.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Memo identifies conflict between reverter right and lender security interest
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly identifies the conflict between the Authority's reverter right and Bayside Federal's lender protections. Top-Risk Register items 1 and 2 flag that the reverter forfeits improvements without compensation and is not subordinate to the leasehold mortgage, lacking an independent lender cure for milestone defaults; the Executive Summary states Bayside requires this as a condition of closing and that the Term Sheet's New Lease right is materially narrower. Section III.B provides a detailed side-by-side comparison of Term Sheet lender protections versus Bayside's Loan Term Sheet §5 requirements (New Lease on any termination, independent lender cure periods, subordination of the reverter), and the Cross-Document Conflict Register entries C11 and C12, Items 2, 8, and 9 document the same. The memo also links the issue to financeability, stating the deal is 'not yet bankable,' that Bayside will not close unless the five items are resolved, and in Section 4.9 ties the reverter to the $285M loan's LTV/appraisal concerns. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Lease subordinates reverter right to leasehold mortgage/lender protections
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease extensively protects the construction lender against the reverter right. Article 9 conditions exercise of the Reverter Right on: notice to each Leasehold Mortgagee (Sections 9.4(e), 9.5(a), 10.2); expiration of all Lender Cure Periods, including a 180-day lender cure period during which the lender may advance funds, exercise completion guaranties, or designate a replacement developer/general contractor/property manager (Section 10.3(c)); and exhaustion of the lender's New Lease right (Section 10.5). Section 9.9 expressly subordinates the Reverter Right to each Leasehold Mortgage and declares any exercise in violation void. Section 9.6 provides that the reverter is conditioned on payment of the Purchase Price to Tenant/lender and that a New Lease alternative defeats the Purchase Price. These provisions satisfy the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Memo identifies conflict between ROFR and lender foreclosure rights
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo repeatedly and explicitly flags the conflict between the Authority's right of first refusal and the lender's foreclosure/assignment rights. It appears in the Top-Risk Register (#7: 'Recorded 2019 right of first refusal has no foreclosure or mortgagee carve-out' conflicting with Bayside's §5.6 demand that the Lender may foreclose and assign without Landlord consent), in the Cross-Document Conflict Register (C10), in the Issue Register (Item 12: 'Recorded 2019 right of first refusal contains, expressly, no carve-out for foreclosure, deed in lieu, or mortgagee assignment... Directly conflicts with Bayside §5.6. Require a recorded amendment and subordination as a condition precedent'), in the Executive Summary's list of closing prerequisites, in the negotiation sequencing (§8.2, item 5), and in Appendix B (ROFR row and Permitted Exceptions). The memo also treats the amendment/subordination as a condition precedent in the draft lease (§§2.7(d), 11.4(e)). This fully satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Lease carves out lender foreclosure/transfers from ROFR
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 11.4(e) expressly excludes from the Authority's Right of First Refusal any assignment, transfer, or disposition in connection with a Leasehold Mortgage, including foreclosure, deed in lieu of foreclosure, exercise of any remedy thereunder, or any transfer by a Leasehold Mortgagee or its designee. Section 10.7 likewise treats foreclosure and related transfers as Permitted Transfers expressly excluded from the ROFR, and Section 2.7(d) requires recording an amendment to the existing recorded Declaration of ROFR to exclude Leasehold Mortgage foreclosures and lender transfers. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Memo identifies 12-month force majeure cap may be insufficient for coastal waterfront project
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo raises precisely this concern. In Issue Register Item 5, it flags that the force majeure provision is "day-for-day but capped at 18 months in the aggregate... the list omits... coastal storm risk" and warns that "One 18-month storm or permitting delay exhausts the entire extension," recommending "Uncapped extensions for Landlord/City delay, ELUR review, unknown contamination, and third-party challenges; expanded FM list." Appendix B repeats this departure ("18-month aggregate cap" vs. "Uncapped... A single event should not exhaust total relief"), and Appendix A traces the underlying "12 months plus 6 months for permitting; 18-month aggregate cap." The project is a waterfront development with flood-zone context elsewhere (BFE 12' NAVD88, coastal storm risk). Thus the memo both identifies the aggregate cap as inadequate for coastal construction and recommends extensions beyond the cap, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Memo recommends force majeure cover climate-related events
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo identifies that the force majeure list omits 'coastal storm risk' and recommends an 'expanded FM list,' effectively recommending that force majeure cover climate-related coastal storm events. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Memo identifies CPI rent reset gap period ambiguity
criteria_results.reasoning: The criterion requires the memo to flag the structural ambiguity that while fixed 2.5% compounding escalations apply for Years 1-15 and CPI resets occur every 10 years starting at Year 16, the term sheet is silent on what governs annual increases during the periods between CPI reset dates (e.g., Years 16-25). Reviewing the memo, the CPI reset analysis in Section 4.8 and Issue Register Item 25 identifies three defects: (1) no cap, (2) a ratchet effect from the 'greater of' structure, and (3) an 'internal ambiguity' about whether the measurement anchor is the Lease Commencement Date or the Rent Commencement Date (a three-year difference). None of these addresses the gap-period problem—namely what annual escalation (if any) governs rent during the years between CPI reset dates. The memo describes the reset structure and computes rent at reset years (16, 26, 36, etc.) but never states that the term sheet is silent on annual increases in the intervening years like Years 16-25. The 'measurement period ambiguous' language in Item 25 refers only to the anchor-date question, not the interstitial escalation gap. Thus the specific structural ambiguity described in the criterion is not identified.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Lease specifies interim escalation mechanism between CPI resets
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease provides CPI resets only on the first day of Rent Year 16 and every tenth Rent Year thereafter (26, 36, etc.), but it does not specify any interim escalation mechanism for the years between those reset dates. Sections 4.2 and 4.3 do not provide for continued fixed annual increases or another method of adjusting Base Rent between CPI resets, so rent would remain flat between resets. This fails the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Memo identifies that percentage rent breakpoint is not indexed
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo squarely identifies the fixed percentage-rent breakpoint issue. It appears as Top-Risk Register item #5 ('Percentage rent breakpoint fixed at $28.5M for 99 years — Converts a negotiated participation into an escalating share of gross receipts; at 3% revenue growth the percentage rent rises from $30,000 to $8.0M a year over the Term'). Section III.D analyzes it in depth, stating over a 99-year term 'that is not a participation; it is a permanent share of gross receipts,' and Section 4.7 provides a fixed-vs-indexed sensitivity table through Rent Year 96. Item 23 of the Issue Register records the same concern. The memo recommends indexing: primary position tying the Breakpoint to Base Rent (preserving the 10:1 relationship), with fallbacks of CPI indexation, 50% CPI, periodic resets to the greater of the fixed number and 85% of stabilized revenue every tenth Rent Year, or a $2M aggregate cap. This satisfies all elements of the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Lease indexes or periodically resets the percentage rent breakpoint
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 5.3 of the draft sets the Breakpoint for Rent Year 6 at $28,500,000, but expressly provides that for each subsequent Rent Year the Breakpoint equals $28,500,000 multiplied by the ratio of the Base Rent payable for that Rent Year to the Initial Base Rent, with a floor of $28,500,000. This ties the Breakpoint to Base Rent escalation (including the 2.5% fixed escalations and CPI resets), so it grows over the 99-year Term rather than remaining fixed. The accompanying drafting note confirms the intent to convert the Term Sheet's static breakpoint into an indexation mechanism. The criterion is therefore satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Memo identifies tax abatement timing misalignment
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo squarely addresses the tax abatement timing issue in Section III.C (and cross-references in Top-Risk Register Item 3, Issue Register Items 20 and 25, and the Cross-Document Conflict Register C18). It identifies that Term Sheet §10 commences the 15-year abatement on the Lease Commencement Date (October 1, 2025) while the Rent Commencement Date is up to 36 months later (October 1, 2028), and expressly notes the consequence that three of the fifteen abatement years are consumed during construction before any revenue is generated. It further quantifies the loss (~$18.1M nominal through 2043, ~$4.2M during construction) and proposes moving commencement to the Rent Commencement Date. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Lease specifies tax abatement commences upon Rent Commencement or first CO
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 6.2(a) expressly provides that the fifteen Abatement Years begin on the Rent Commencement Date (defined in Section 2.4 by reference to a 36-month outside date or substantial CO issuance for 60% of the Residential Tower and 50% of the Project), not the Lease Commencement Date. Section 6.2(b) further addresses the construction-period gap by basing taxes during the Construction Period on the actual land-only assessed value, without applying post-development phase-in percentages. The drafting note confirms the deliberate shift from the Term Sheet's Lease Commencement Date trigger to the Rent Commencement Date to avoid imposing post-development taxes during construction. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Memo addresses unconscionability of improvement forfeiture under reverter
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo squarely addresses the unconscionability/disproportionality of the improvement forfeiture. Section III.A analyzes the reverter as an inverted penalty (roughly 111:1 ratio at Milestone 3, ~$317M forfeited against ~$2.85M/year delay loss), and Section VI lays out Connecticut equitable doctrines disfavoring forfeiture (Restatement §§ 227(1), 229; penalty doctrine under § 356(1); unjust enrichment and constitutional arguments). The memo also recommends alternatives consistent with the criterion — a Purchase Price equal to the greater of appraised fair market value and Tenant's Unreimbursed Hard Costs, with no payment meaning no termination, plus a 90%-complete safe harbor. Appendix B and the Issue Register (Items 1–3) reiterate these positions.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Lease mitigates improvement forfeiture with buyout or reimbursement
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease contains a robust set of compensation mechanisms mitigating forfeiture of improvements upon exercise of the Reverter Right. Section 9.6 obligates Landlord to pay a Purchase Price equal to the greater of the Fair Market Value of the Improvements or Tenant's Unreimbursed Hard Costs (less insurance proceeds, documented damages, and third-party recoveries), with an appraisal procedure in Section 9.7. Section 9.8 expressly states improvements shall not revert to Landlord without payment and deems any contrary provision modified; Section 14.5(c) confirms that on a Reverter Right termination the Improvements do not vest in Landlord until the Purchase Price is paid (or a Leasehold Mortgagee takes a New Lease under Section 10.5, in which case Improvements pass to the new tenant). Sections 9.9/9.10 further subordinate the Reverter Right and reform any penalty/forfeiture. Although Section 14.5(a) allows uncompensated vesting on a non-Reverter Event of Default termination, that is subject to Leasehold Mortgagee rights and is outside the reverter scenario the criterion targets. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Memo identifies missing estoppel certificate framework
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly flags the absence of an estoppel/SNDA/recognition framework, stating that the Term Sheet provides no mechanism for landlord estoppels and that this is critical because a 99-year ground lease will be refinanced repeatedly. It also includes Issue 11 and a lease section (§10.9) addressing the gap. Although it does not expressly mention the construction loan term sheet in the estoppel item, it sufficiently identifies the missing estoppel certificate framework and its importance to refinancing.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Lease includes estoppel certificate provision with specified timeframe
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes an estoppel certificate provision in Section 17.6 requiring each party, including the Authority/Landlord, to execute and deliver an estoppel certificate within ten (10) Business Days after request. Section 10.9 also requires Landlord to deliver estoppel certificates within ten (10) Business Days in financing contexts. Thus the criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Lease estoppel provision includes deemed-approval mechanism
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 17.6 of the lease includes an estoppel certificate provision requiring delivery within 10 Business Days, and expressly states that failure to deliver within that period constitutes an estoppel in favor of the requesting party as to the matters stated unless a written objection is delivered. This is a deemed-confirmation mechanism applicable to the Authority as a party.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_012: Memo identifies lack of affordable housing implementation detail
criteria_results.reasoning: Item 26 of the Issue Register expressly identifies that the 15% affordable housing covenant lacks implementation detail — citing the omission of recalculation on a change in unit count, income verification, monitoring entity, enforcement rights, unit distribution, and consequences of non-compliance — and states the recorded declaration is unenforceable as a practical matter, with a full covenant drafted to cure these gaps. The memo also notes in Item 45 and conflict C20 that the 15% obligation cannot even be quantified because the unit count is 'to be determined.' This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_012: Lease includes substantive affordable housing compliance provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.6 of the lease contains detailed affordable housing provisions that address multiple prongs of the criterion: (a) calculation of the 15% (based on total dwelling units per the Project Program, with recalculation upon any change in unit count and proportionate distribution among unit types); (b) income verification/eligibility (requires income verification procedures consistent with HUD guidance, defines AMI by reference to HUD's New Haven-Milford MSA publication); (c) compliance monitoring (annual rent roll and income certification within 90 days after Rent Commencement Date and annually thereafter, books-and-records inspection rights, independent monitor on a finding of material non-compliance); and (d) consequences of non-compliance (notice, 90-day cure extendable to 180 days, remedies limited to specific performance and actual damages, with express exclusion of the Reverter Right and Security Deposit draw). It also incorporates the recorded Declaration of Restrictive Covenants (Vol. 408, Pg. 230) as satisfied by Section 3.6. The lease thus goes well beyond merely restating the 15% requirement, satisfying at least two (in fact four) of the enumerated prongs. Minor gaps (e.g., no explicit treatment of subsidy expiration) do not affect the verdict.

criteria_results.title: Lease identifies correct Landlord name and entity type
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease identifies the Landlord as "CITY OF PORT CALLOWAY REDEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY, a public body corporate and politic organized and existing under the provisions of the Connecticut General Statutes, Section 8-125 et seq." This matches the criterion's required name and entity type exactly, both in the preamble and consistently throughout (e.g., Section 15.6(a) restates the entity form and § 8-125 authority).

criteria_results.title: Lease identifies correct Tenant name and entity type
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease's preamble identifies the Tenant as "MERIDIAN GATEWAY HOLDINGS LLC, a Delaware limited liability company," which matches the required name and entity type exactly.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct property address and APN
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover page identifies the Premises as "10-30 Pier Street, Port Calloway, Connecticut 06801" with "Assessor's Parcel No. 127-003-0045," and the same address and APN are repeated in Recital A, Section 2.1 context, and Exhibit A. Both the address and the APN match the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct parcel size
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly references the parcel size as 'approximately 3.2 acres (139,392 square feet)' in Recital A, and Exhibit A states 'Containing 139,392 square feet, or 3.200 acres, more or less, as determined by the Tax Assessor.' The criterion is satisfied. (The drafting notes discussing an alternative surveyed area of ~139,474.95 sq. ft. do not negate the required reference, and the correct 3.2 acre/139,392 sq. ft. figure is clearly stated.)

criteria_results.title: Lease states correct lease term of 99 years from October 1, 2025
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 2.2 states a 99-year Term, with the Commencement Date intended to be October 1, 2025, and the Expiration Date intended to be September 30, 2124. The definition of Commencement Date also confirms the parties intend October 1, 2025. This matches the required 99-year term from October 1, 2025, with the equivalent September 30, 2124 expiration.

criteria_results.title: Lease states correct initial annual base rent of $2,850,000
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 4.1 of the lease expressly states initial annual Base Rent of Two Million Eight Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars ($2,850,000), payable in equal monthly installments of Two Hundred Thirty-Seven Thousand Five Hundred Dollars ($237,500) in advance on the first day of each calendar month. The monthly figure is consistent with the annual amount ($2,850,000 / 12 = $237,500), and the same figures are carried through the rent schedule, Security Deposit calculation (24 × $237,500 = $5,700,000), and Remediation Credit. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct Rent Commencement Date definition
criteria_results.reasoning: The criterion requires the Rent Commencement Date to be the earlier of (a) 36 months after the Lease Commencement Date and (b) issuance of the first certificate of occupancy for any portion of the project. The agent's Section 2.4 defines clause (a) correctly (36 months after Commencement Date), but clause (b) is materially different: it requires certificates of occupancy for not less than 60% of the Residential Tower's Rentable Area AND not less than 50% of the aggregate Rentable Area of the Project, and expressly excludes temporary/ancillary certificates (leasing offices, parking, etc.). The agent's own drafting note acknowledges it deliberately substituted a substantial-completion threshold for the 'any portion of the Project' standard. Because clause (b) does not match the required 'first certificate of occupancy for any portion of the project' trigger, the definition is incorrect under the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct fixed rent escalation: 2.5% compounding every 5 years
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes a fixed rent escalation in Section 4.2: 2.5% annual compounding applied every five years. It specifies Year 6-10 Base Rent of $3,224,513/year and Year 11-15 Base Rent of $3,648,241/year, calculated as $2,850,000 × (1.025)^5 and × (1.025)^10. These amounts are essentially the same as the criterion's $3,224,500 and $3,648,200 figures and are consistent with the required formula.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes CPI rent reset mechanism starting Year 16
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 4.3 of the lease establishes a CPI-based rent reset commencing on the first day of Rent Year 16 and every tenth Rent Year thereafter (Years 26, 36, 46, 56, 66, 76, 86, 96). At each reset, Base Rent becomes the greater of (a) the Initial Base Rent compounded at 2.5% annually, or (b) the Initial Base Rent adjusted by cumulative CPI increase, with a 3% cap and a floor at the prior year's rent. Section 1.1 defines CPI as the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, Northeast Region (BLS Series ID CUUR0100SA0), and Section 4.4 provides CPI mechanics. This matches the criterion: Year 16 commencement, 10-year intervals, CPI-U Northeast Region, greater-of structure using CPI-adjusted initial base rent.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct percentage rent terms
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 5 of the lease provides Percentage Rent equal to 2.0% of Gross Revenues in excess of the Breakpoint, commencing with Rent Year 6 and continuing for the balance of the Term. The Breakpoint for Rent Year 6 is $28,500,000, indexed thereafter in proportion to Base Rent (with a $28,500,000 floor), which the criterion expressly permits ('whether $28,500,000 fixed or indexed'). Payment timing under Section 5.4 is annually, within 90 days after the end of each Rent Year (or within 90 days after termination for a partial year), accompanied by a certified statement of Gross Revenues. All three required elements—2.0% rate, Year 6 commencement, and 90-day annual payment—are present and consistent. Although the lease measures the commencement by 'Rent Year' (running from the Rent Commencement Date) rather than 'Lease Year,' the lease clearly and consistently defines these terms and discloses the distinction, so the rate, commencement year, and payment timing are not materially incorrect.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct remediation credit of $1,800,000
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 8.4 of the lease establishes a Remediation Credit of $1,800,000, applied against the first monthly Base Rent installments due after the Rent Commencement Date: months 1–7 reduced to zero (7 × $237,500 = $1,662,500) and month 8 reduced by $137,500 (with Tenant paying the remaining $100,000), totaling exactly $1,800,000 — i.e., approximately 7.5 months of rent. The amount is correct and the application mechanism is fully specified, matching the criterion precisely. (The section also adds flexible-application and reconciliation features, but these do not detract from the required mechanism.)

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct security deposit amount and form (LOC)
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease in Article 7 requires a $5,700,000 security deposit in the form of an irrevocable standby letter of credit, issued by a bank with a minimum long-term unsecured credit rating of A- from S&P Global Ratings or A3 from Moody's. This matches the criterion exactly.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes correct security deposit reduction mechanism
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 7.4 expressly provides that the $5,700,000 letter-of-credit security deposit reduces to $2,850,000 upon satisfaction of Reduction Conditions, which include certificates of occupancy for at least 90% of the Project's aggregate Rentable Area and maintenance of an Occupancy Rate of not less than 90% for twenty-four (24) consecutive full calendar months. Both the reduced amount ($2,850,000, equal to twelve months' initial Base Rent) and the 90%/24-month occupancy threshold match the criterion. The extra condition regarding certificates of occupancy does not alter or misstate the required occupancy threshold or dollar amount, and Section 7.4(c)-(d) supply a detailed definition of Occupancy Rate and the mechanism for effecting the reduction, so the reduction mechanism is present and materially correct.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Milestone 1: construction commencement within 18 months (by April 1, 2027)
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 9.1 of the lease expressly establishes Milestone 1 as 'Commencement of Construction' (defined as physical pouring of footings for at least one building following issuance of all necessary permits), with a Milestone Date of 18 months after the Commencement Date, shown parenthetically as April 1, 2027 based on an October 1, 2025 Commencement Date. The deadline is correct and not materially erroneous.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Milestone 2: structural frame within 42 months (by April 1, 2029)
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 9.1's milestone table expressly lists Milestone No. 2 as "Completion of Structural Frame — Topping out of the structural frame of the Residential Tower" with a Milestone Date of 42 months (April 1, 2029), measured from the Commencement Date (assumed October 1, 2025), with the parenthetical date adjusting automatically if the actual Commencement Date differs. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Milestone 3: Phase 1 substantial completion within 60 months (by October 1, 2030)
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 9.1's Milestone table expressly includes Milestone 3 — 'Substantial Completion of Phase 1' (certificate of occupancy for the Residential Tower and ground-floor retail) — with a Milestone Date of 60 months after the Commencement Date, indicated as October 1, 2030 assuming an October 1, 2025 commencement. The milestone is present and the deadline is correct (60 months / approximately October 1, 2030), and Section 9.1 further provides for adjustment of the parenthetical date if the Commencement Date differs.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Milestone 4: Phase 2 substantial completion within 84 months (by October 1, 2032)
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 9.1 includes Milestone 4 requiring Substantial Completion of Phase 2 (certificate of occupancy for the Office Building) within 84 months, with the corresponding date of October 1, 2032 assuming the intended October 1, 2025 Commencement Date. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes force majeure extension provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 9.3 expressly provides force majeure extensions for Milestone Dates, including an aggregate 18-month extension allocated as 12 months for Force Majeure Events generally and 6 additional months for government permitting delays, with no cap for certain Landlord/City/DEEP delays. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes reverter right provisions for Milestones 1 and 3
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes a reverter right in Article 9 tied to failure to achieve Milestone 1 or Milestone 3, subject to extensions. Section 9.5 provides for a written Reverter Notice and a 180-day cure period, with exercise only after cure periods expire. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes leasehold mortgage permission for construction financing
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 10 of the lease, particularly Section 10.1 ('Right to Encumber'), expressly permits Tenant to grant one or more Leasehold Mortgages encumbering its leasehold interest without Landlord's consent, notice, or fee, and Section 10.7/10.9 address foreclosure and refinancing. The lease also defines the Construction Loan (Bayside Federal Lending Corp., $285,000,000) and references the pledge of membership interests required by that Construction Loan, confirming that leasehold mortgage financing for construction is expressly authorized.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes SNDA framework with the Authority
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly provides an SNDA framework: it defines SNDA, makes delivery of an executed SNDA by Landlord and the Leasehold Mortgagee a condition precedent in Section 2.7(h), requires Landlord to execute an SNDA in favor of each Leasehold Mortgagee under Section 10.9, attaches the form as Exhibit D, and also addresses fee mortgage subordination in Section 15.7.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes New Lease right for lender if ground lease is terminated
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes Article 10.5, which expressly grants each Leasehold Mortgagee (or its designee) the right to obtain a New Lease if the ground lease is terminated for any reason, including Tenant default. The New Lease is on the same terms and conditions for the remainder of the Term, subject to curing monetary defaults within 60 days and non-monetary defaults within 90 days (or commencing cure within 90 days and diligently pursuing completion). This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease requires Authority to provide lender copies of default notices
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 10.2 (Notices to Leasehold Mortgagee) expressly requires that, simultaneously with delivery to Tenant of any notice of default, notice of termination, Reverter Notice, notice of Landlord's default, or any other material notice, Landlord (the Authority) shall deliver a copy of the same to each Leasehold Mortgagee. It further provides that no notice to Tenant is effective unless a copy is simultaneously delivered to each Leasehold Mortgagee. This is reinforced by Section 16.6 (Landlord shall give each Leasehold Mortgagee the notices required by Section 10.2 in respect of any Tenant default) and Section 9.5(a) (Reverter Notice delivered simultaneously to each Leasehold Mortgagee). The lease thus satisfies the criterion that the Authority must send copies of all default notices to the leasehold mortgagee simultaneously with delivery to Tenant.

criteria_results.title: Lease prohibits voluntary surrender without lender consent
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 10.6(a) expressly provides that, for so long as any Leasehold Mortgage remains in effect, 'Landlord shall not accept a voluntary surrender, cancellation, or termination of this Lease from Tenant without the prior written consent of each Leasehold Mortgagee,' and Section 10.6(c) makes any purported surrender without such consent void. The lease is therefore not silent and does not permit surrender without lender consent; it satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes ELUR acknowledgment and compliance obligations
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly references the ELUR recorded March 22, 2018, at Volume 412, Page 88 in Recital B and in the definition of 'Environmental Laws'/'Applicable Law.' It imposes compliance obligations in Section 3.9(a) ('Tenant shall comply, and shall cause the Project to comply, with the ELUR and with all Environmental Laws'), and specifically acknowledges both the ground-floor residential prohibition and the engineered barrier requirement for areas of ground disturbance. Exhibit B also lists the ELUR as a Permitted Exception. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease specifies Tenant's remaining remediation responsibility of $600,000
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 8.3(a)–(b) sets the Estimated Remediation Cost at $2,400,000 and allocates it 75% to Landlord / 25% to Tenant, expressly capping Tenant's share of Remediation Costs at $600,000 in the aggregate. Section 8.4 separately grants Tenant an $1,800,000 Remediation Credit against Base Rent (75% of the estimate). Together these provisions specify the Authority's $1,800,000 contribution and Tenant's remaining $600,000 responsibility, with excess-cost allocation rules in Section 8.3(c) and reconciliation in Section 8.4(c). The amounts are correct and consistent with the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes comprehensive insurance requirements
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 12 of the lease contains all required coverages: (a) CGL with $10M per occurrence / $20M aggregate (§12.1(a)); (b) All-Risk Property Insurance on a full replacement-cost basis with agreed-amount and ordinance/law coverage (§12.1(c)); (c) Builder's Risk on a completed-value basis during construction (§12.1(d)); (d) Flood Insurance for full replacement cost, expressly requiring more than NFIP limits (§12.1(e)); (e) Environmental/Pollution Legal Liability at $5M per occurrence / $10M aggregate (§12.1(f)); and (f) Workers' Compensation per Connecticut statute plus Employer's Liability (§12.1(g)). Section 12.2 names Landlord (the Authority) and the City as additional insureds on the CGL, umbrella, and excess liability policies, and provides for Landlord as loss payee on the property/builder's risk/flood policies (subject to the Leasehold Mortgagee's priority). The additional-insured designation on the property policies is handled through a loss-payee arrangement rather than additional-insured status, and is hedged to protect lender recovery—at most a minor, single deviation, well within the criterion's tolerance (FAIL only if more than two requirements are missing).

criteria_results.title: Lease includes triple-net structure for taxes and operating costs
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly states in Section 4.5 that it is a triple-net lease, and it separately obligates Tenant to pay all real property taxes, assessments, and governmental charges (Article 6), utilities (Section 6.5), insurance (Article 12), and maintenance and repair costs (Article 14). Although the tax abatement program modifies the timing and amount of certain tax obligations, the overall cost structure remains triple-net.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes tax abatement phase-in schedule
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 6.2 of the lease expressly sets forth the tax abatement phase-in schedule in a table: Abatement Years 1–5 at 25% of full assessed value, Years 6–10 at 50%, Years 11–15 at 75%, and Year 16 and thereafter at 100%. It also includes estimated annual tax amounts, the statutory basis, Landlord/City obligations to implement the Abatement Program, and a remedy for failure. The required 15-year phase-in is fully included and referenced throughout (e.g., Sections 2.7(e), 6.2, and Exhibit G). The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes permitted use restrictions consistent with term sheet
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.3 expressly permits all five required uses: (a) residential apartments, (b) Class A office, (c) ground-floor retail, (d) restaurants including liquor service, and (e) accessory structured/surface/below-grade parking. Section 3.4 expressly prohibits all five required excluded uses: adult entertainment establishments, sale of firearms, pawnshops, gasoline service stations/motor fuel dispensing, and industrial/manufacturing (with warehousing/distribution). Both the permitted and prohibited use lists satisfy the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease requires minimum 8,000 SF publicly accessible open space
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.7 of the lease expressly requires Tenant to design and construct not less than 8,000 square feet of publicly accessible open space on or adjacent to the waterfront (eastern) side of the Premises, designed for public use and connected to the existing public pedestrian promenade along Long Island Sound. Section 3.2 further prohibits any Project modification that would reduce the Public Open Space below 8,000 square feet without Landlord's consent, and Exhibit E (Project Program) restates the 8,000 SF minimum. The requirement is clearly present and satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes assignment/subletting provisions with ROFR
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease includes Article 11 with assignment and subletting provisions and a Right of First Refusal in Section 11.4. The ROFR runs from the Commencement Date through September 30, 2045 (approximately 20 years) and applies to proposed Transfers that are not Permitted Transfers, i.e., assignments to non-affiliated entities. Permitted Transfers exclude affiliate transfers from the ROFR, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes finished floor elevation requirement of at least 15 ft NAVD88
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease references NAVD88 and FEMA Flood Zone AE with a base flood elevation of 12 feet NAVD88, but it does not specify a finished floor elevation requirement of at least 15 feet NAVD88 anywhere in the document.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes default and remedies provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 16 of the lease contains robust default and remedies provisions. It defines multiple Tenant Events of Default — monetary default (10 Business Days after notice), non-monetary default (30 days after notice, with extension for diligent cure), milestone default (cross-referencing Article 9 cure periods), insolvency, and abandonment — each with specified notice and/or cure periods stated in days. It also defines Landlord Events of Default (Section 16.3), including failure to perform material obligations with a 30-day cure period after written notice (extendable where cure cannot reasonably be completed in 30 days), breach of representations, wrongful termination/interference, and failure to pay amounts owing within 30 days after demand. Remedies for both parties are set out in Sections 16.2 and 16.4. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes indemnification provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease contains express indemnification provisions. Section 8.7(a) requires Tenant to indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Landlord (the Authority) and its commissioners, officers, employees, and agents from claims arising out of Tenant's breach of Article 8, releases of hazardous materials caused by Tenant or its contractors/subtenants, and 'any construction, operation, or condition on the Premises during the Term' not attributable to pre-commencement conditions—language broad enough to cover claims arising from Tenant's use and occupancy. Section 12.1(a) reinforces this by requiring contractual liability insurance for the lease indemnities, and Section 12.2 requires Landlord be named an additional insured. Complementary Landlord-side indemnities (e.g., Sections 3.7(c), 8.7(b)) and survival of indemnities (Section 8.7(c)) are also included. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes casualty and condemnation provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 13 of the lease comprehensively addresses both casualty and condemnation. Section 13.1 imposes on Tenant an obligation to restore the Improvements to substantially their pre-Casualty condition using insurance proceeds, with Sections 13.2–13.3 providing rent abatement and termination rights. Section 13.4 expressly allocates the condemnation Award among Landlord (fee interest), Tenant (leasehold and Improvements, relocation/business interruption damages), and Leasehold Mortgagees, with unresolved allocation determined by appraisal; Section 13.5 addresses temporary and permanent partial takings, restoration, and equitable rent reduction. Both required elements—Tenant's rebuild obligation and condemnation award allocation—are present.

criteria_results.title: Memo includes at least three negotiation recommendations identifying counterparty and specific lease provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo contains numerous negotiation recommendations that identify the counterparty and specific provisions. Section 8.2 ("Negotiation posture on the five critical items") expressly frames the recommendations for the call with Howard Koss of Pryor Whitfield & Koss (the Authority's/Landlord's counsel) and prioritizes five items by name and provision: (1) the reverter (Term Sheet §9 / Lease §§9.4–9.10), (2) the tax abatement commencement date (TS §10 / Lease §6.2), (3) percentage-rent indexation (TS §6 / Lease §5.3), (4) the legal description and mechanics' lien (Exh. A; TS §13 / Lease §§2.7(c), 15.4), and (5) the ROFR amendment (TS §11 / Lease §11.4(e)). Each of the Six Critical Issues in Section III ends with a stated negotiating position tied to specific lease sections, the Issue Register gives 47 items with a "Lease §" response column, and Appendix B is a complete departure list framed as an agenda for the Board and negotiation. Far more than three qualifying recommendations are present.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes lender's right to foreclose/assign to qualified transferee
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 10.7 ("Foreclosure and Assignment") expressly grants each Leasehold Mortgagee the unconditional right to foreclose its Leasehold Mortgage (by judicial foreclosure, power of sale, or otherwise), to accept a deed in lieu of foreclosure, and to assign the Lease to a qualified transferee at or following foreclosure or deed-in-lieu transfer without Landlord's prior consent and without triggering any right of first refusal. It further provides that any such transferee must meet financial and experience qualifications substantially similar to those required of Tenant as of the Commencement Date, as reasonably determined by Landlord, and that Landlord shall not unreasonably withhold recognition and shall not require any fee. The output therefore squarely satisfies the criterion—granting foreclosure and assignment rights coupled with reasonable transferee qualification standards. Related protections (Section 10.5 New Lease, Section 10.3 Lender Cure Periods, Section 11.1(b) Permitted Transfer, and the SNDA in Exhibit D) further reinforce these rights, but the core requirement is met by Section 10.7.

criteria_results.title: Lease identifies the construction loan from Bayside Federal
criteria_results.reasoning: The lease expressly identifies the construction loan from Bayside Federal Lending Corp. in the definition of 'Construction Loan,' stating an original principal amount of $285,000,000 and referencing the May 28, 2025 construction loan term sheet. It also lists Bayside Federal Lending Corp. as the Leasehold Mortgagee for notice purposes.

criteria_results.title: Lease includes Tenant's obligation to comply with affordable housing covenant
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.6 of the lease, titled 'Affordable Housing Covenant,' expressly requires that not less than fifteen percent (15%) of residential dwelling units be designated as Affordable Housing Units available to households earning at or below 80% of Area Median Income (AMI), at rents not exceeding the applicable HUD maximum rent, 'for the duration of the Term.' It further provides AMI definition, recalculation, monitoring, enforcement, and cure provisions. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Both deliverable files are produced
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent produced two distinct deliverables: (1) a complete Ground Lease Agreement (ground-lease-agreement.docx), with recitals, 18 articles, exhibits, and signature blocks; and (2) a separate cover/drafting issues memorandum (drafting-issues-memo.docx), addressing risks, conflicts, recomputations, and an issue register. Both required deliverables are present and substantive.
